@graph.description: A backtest is one roll of the dice. Monte Carlo simulation in trading rolls it a thousand times — here's what the fan tells you and how to set size from it.
@graph.headline: Monte Carlo Simulation for Traders: What It Is, How It Works, and How to Size From It

acceptedAnswer.text: It's a resampling technique: your strategy's actual trade-by-trade results are re-dealt — shuffled in order, with trades skipped and execution varied — thousands of times to build a distribution of plausible equity curves. The output is a fan chart from which you read median vs P10/P90 paths, the drawdown distribution, and the probability of hitting a ruin threshold you define. It prices sequence risk; it doesn't predict your future.

mainEntity.name: What is Monte Carlo simulation in trading?

acceptedAnswer.text: A backtest shows one sequence: what your trades did in the exact order they happened to occur. Monte Carlo simulation shows what those same trades could do across a thousand different orderings — the set of alternate histories consistent with your data. Backtesting estimates the edge; Monte Carlo estimates how bumpy the ride to that edge could be. You need both, in that order.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between backtesting and Monte Carlo simulation?

acceptedAnswer.text: Practitioners often use 1,000 as the working standard — enough paths for percentile and ruin-probability estimates to stabilize. Use 10,000 for serious studies where tail estimates matter, and treat ~100 as a quick rough read only.

mainEntity.name: How many Monte Carlo simulations should I run?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. It assumes your trade sample represents the future and then explores what different orderings of that sample could produce. If the sample is overfit or the market regime changes, the fan's answers are conditional on a world that no longer exists. It's a risk-pricing tool, not a crystal ball.

mainEntity.name: Can Monte Carlo simulation predict future trading results?

acceptedAnswer.text: No — this is the garbage-in rule. Monte Carlo resamples the trades you give it; if those trades are the product of curve-fitting rather than a real edge, all a thousand paths are fantasies of the same mirage. Validate out-of-sample first; only then put the sample through the fan.

mainEntity.name: Does Monte Carlo work if my strategy is overfit?

acceptedAnswer.text: Run the fan at several risk-per-trade levels (e.g. 0.5%, 1%, 2%, 3%) and compare the ruin probabilities and 90th-percentile drawdowns. Because doubling size multiplies severe-drawdown odds far more than it lifts returns, pick the largest size whose worst plausible path you can genuinely survive. Use position sizing for the lot math and risk of ruin for the closed-form comparison.

mainEntity.name: How do I use Monte Carlo results to set position size?

acceptedAnswer.text: First define ruin — the account-loss line (say 30%) at which you'd stop trading the strategy. Practitioners often treat around 5% probability of crossing that line as roughly acceptable and more than 10% as a reason to avoid or resize. Those are third-party rules of thumb, not guarantees; the number only means something attached to a threshold you've truly committed to.

mainEntity.name: What is an acceptable probability of ruin?

acceptedAnswer.text: Because your backtest drew one lucky ordering of history. The fan explores orderings where losers cluster early and streaks stretch longer — sequences your sample contains but your single realized order happened to avoid. The worst paths aren't pessimistic; they're the honest price of the same trades dealt in a different order.
